intro: Each town runs its own elections. The town's registrars of voters handle voter sign-up and polling places, and the town clerk handles absentee ballots. The Secretary of the State oversees elections statewide.

elections.name: State election
elections.what: Federal, state, and some local offices, such as judge of probate and registrar of voters. Your exact ballot depends on where you live.

dates.label: Absentee ballots start going out
dates.detail: Any voter can vote by absentee ballot. No reason is needed. Apply online at MyVote.CT.gov, or mail or hand in an application to your town clerk.

src.label: CT Secretary of the State, Absentee Voting

dates.label: Last day to register to vote
dates.detail: Register in person at your registrar of voters from 9 am to 8 pm, online by 11:59 pm, or by mail with a form postmarked by Oct. 16. After this date, you can still register and vote the same day during early voting or on Election Day.

src.label: CT Secretary of the State, Voter Registration Deadlines for Nov. 3, 2026

dates.label: Early voting
dates.detail: Vote in person at your town's early voting site, 10 am to 6 pm every day, including weekends. Hours are 8 am to 8 pm on Tuesday, Oct. 27 and Thursday, Oct. 29. You can also register and vote the same day at the early voting site.

src.label: CT Secretary of the State, 2026 Election Calendar
CT Secretary of the State, Voter Registration Deadlines

dates.label: Absentee ballot request deadline
dates.detail: Last day to request an absentee ballot.

src.label: CT Secretary of the State, Absentee Voting

dates.label: Election Day
dates.detail: Polls open 6 am to 8 pm at your assigned polling place. Absentee ballots must be received by 8 pm. Return them by mail, your town's drop box, or to the town clerk. If you are not registered, go to your town's same-day registration site, not your polling place.

CT Secretary of the State, Same-Day Registration

id_rule.text: Poll workers will ask for ID, but you do not need a photo ID. A photo ID with your name and address works, or a current bill, bank statement, paycheck, or government document with your name and address. Other pre-printed ID, like a Social Security card, also works. If you have no ID, you can usually sign a form saying who you are and still vote. Some first-time voters who registered by mail have stricter rules.
